description: ¡Hola! Somos el equipo Los juggernauts. Vamos a resolver el desafío de ser detectives de tendencias del sistema terrestre usando datos de la NASA para analizar cambios ambientales.
summary: We built Cusco Earth Lab, a geospatial intelligence platform that sets out to answer four questions about Earth’s changing systems: what is shifting, where, by how much, and whether the signal is statistically significant. It fuses NASA Landsat 8/9 observations in Google Earth Engine, covering vegetation indices, land surface temperature, active-fire detections and precipitation, and ties them to El Niño 3.4 anomalies to separate natural climate cycles from lasting change. Users pin down a study quadrant by longitude, latitude, radius and date, and the system spins up a trend map, a time series and a plain-language verdict within seconds. A 3D terrain twin built on SRTM elevation layers a decade of fire detections over the relief. Basic and Expert modes bridge communities and scientists. Every result stays traceable to open NASA data and can be reproduced. Looking ahead, we aim to scale this into a real-time early-warning layer that picks up ecosystem degradation, feeds forecasting models and lets authorities act before biomass loss, wildfires and water stress spill over into food and social crises.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Cusco Earth Lab lets anyone pick a study quadrant (longitude, latitude, radius in meters, date) and see what is changing there, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. For each quadrant the app builds annual series of vegetation (NDVI/EVI, 250 m), net primary productivity, land surface temperature, rainfall (CHIRPS) and fire days, then fits a Theil-Sen slope. It also reports the share of pixels with significant greening or browning, so opposite trends do not cancel out in a regional average. Results are shown next to El Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature to separate natural cycles from lasting change. A 3D terrain viewer overlays 2016-2026 fire detections on real relief.

BENEFITS AND EXPECTED IMPACT

Communities, municipalities and emergency offices get a clear, evidence-based answer instead of raw maps. Cusco logged 275 wildfires and about 7,500 ha burned by late September 2025, and the regional emergency office attributes 99% to human action, while NOAA expects a strong-to-very-strong El Niño through early 2027. A tool that flags where vegetation is degrading, and whether it is significant, supports prevention and planning. The method is open and portable to any region.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Google Earth Engine (JavaScript and Python API) with NASA products and CHIRPS rainfall; SRTM terrain; Python (Pandas, NumPy) for validation against pymannkendall; Three.js for the 3D viewer; Next.js and TypeScript for the web app. Trend images are precomputed as assets, so each quadrant query is a single lightweight reduction with no lag.

CREATIVITY

We link a quadrant to a satellite model in a 3D scene, combine statistics with plain-language verdicts, and treat significance per pixel, not only on the mean.

TEAM CONSIDERATIONS

Statistical honesty (we state limits: serial correlation and multiple testing can inflate significance, so pre-whitening and FDR correction are next), usability for experts and non-experts, reproducibility with open data, and local relevance for the Peruvian Andes.

HOW TO USE

  • Cataloged Sites (Cusco): Provides a dropdown menu of 7 historical wildfire events across Cusco (2019–2026), allowing immediate inspection and comparison of major fires across different provinces and elevations without manual setup.
  • Custom Coordinates (New Quadrant): Enables users to input any Longitude, Latitude, Radius (m), and Date to dynamically generate a custom analysis area, ensuring the tool can audit any recent fire or specific parcel beyond the pre-loaded catalog.
  • Spectral Parameter / Index: Switches the map layers between true color, infrared bands, burn severity (dNBR), and bare soil exposure (dBSI), revealing vegetation loss and soil erosion risks that are invisible to the naked eye.
  • Active Quadrant Metrics: Automatically calculates and displays the total burned area in hectares ($\text{dNBR} \ge 0.15$) and mean burn severity, turning visual map observations into objective data for environmental assessments.
  • Biomass Trajectory (2016–2026): Plots a 10-year time series of annual vegetation vigor (NDVI P80) strictly within the burned scar to evaluate baseline ecosystem health before the fire and track natural recovery afterward.
  • SST Evolution – El Niño Region 1+2 (2016–2026): Displays historical Sea Surface Temperature (SST) anomalies off the Peruvian coast to correlate warm El Niño phases with severe Andean droughts and heightened wildfire recurrence in Cusco.
